headline: High risk of shared-repo write conflicts and medium prompt/data leakage via filesystem and git; no critical compliance gap is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes repo files and shares state via a git repo; Gemini CLI also reads/writes repo files and user-provided directories. That creates a plausible file-content injection path if one agent consumes the other’s generated files as trusted instructions. No MCP bridge is documented between them, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF either agent is configured to read the other agent’s output files as instructions, injection becomes active.
IF both agents operate in the same repository without content provenance checks, malicious file content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different working directories.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files as prompts.
Add a manual review step before one agent consumes the other’s output.
Use provenance tags or filename conventions for agent-generated artifacts.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code and files in the working directory, and both can send context to external model APIs. In a shared repo, sensitive code or secrets in files can flow into either backend by default. The profiles do not show a stronger third-party exfiltration path than normal model calls, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF the shared workspace contains secrets or regulated code, both agents can read them.
IF either agent is pointed at the same directory tree, file contents may be transmitted to its model backend.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared workspace.
Use separate clones with least-privilege file access.
Restrict both agents to a narrow subdirectory.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
requires-engineering: enforce redaction before model submission.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider and Gemini CLI both have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and git-state modification, and both share state through the same repo/filesystem. Concurrent edits without locking can overwrite each other or corrupt git history. This is a default-dangerous overlap because both agents can mutate the same mutable resources.
conditions: IF both agents run against the same git repository concurrently, write conflicts are possible.
IF either agent auto-commits while the other is editing, history divergence can occur.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repository at a time.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Require manual merge review after each commit.
requires-engineering: add repository locking in the orchestrator.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can emit code changes and git commits, while Gemini CLI can also act on tool outputs and modify files. If Gemini treats Aider’s output as authoritative, an error can cascade into further edits or commits. The profiles do not prove fully automated downstream actions, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Gemini consumes Aider-generated patches or summaries without verification, mistakes propagate.
IF Aider’s commits are used as ground truth for subsequent edits, errors can compound.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before applying generated patches.
Compare proposed diffs against the original files.
Limit each agent to advisory mode for one step.
Keep a human approval gate before commits.
requires-engineering: add automated diff validation and rollback checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding agents with similar source-code and git-history data classes, and no residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. I therefore see only a small compliance gap risk from ordinary code handling, not a specific regulated-data violation. The other agent is cited because the assessment is pairwise, but no stronger mismatch is evidenced.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared repo, compliance obligations may change.
IF one deployment adds stricter retention or residency rules than the other, the mismatch becomes relevant.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared repository.
Document retention settings for both agents.
Use separate environments for regulated projects.
Review vendor terms before handling sensitive data.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing.
